raw_text:
# Sacubitril/Valsartan in Heart Failure: A Narrative Review

## Introduction

Heart failure (HF) remains a leading cause of morbidity, mortality, and hospitalization worldwide, affecting an estimated 64 million people [1]. Despite advances in neurohormonal blockade with angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitors, angiotensin receptor blockers (ARBs), beta-blockers, and mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists (MRAs), residual risk persists [2]. The introduction of sacubitril/valsartan, the first-in-class angiotensin receptor–neprilysin inhibitor (ARNI), represented a paradigm shift in the pharmacotherapy of HF with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF) [3].

## Mechanism of Action

Neprilysin is a neutral endopeptidase responsible for the degradation of several vasoactive peptides, including natriuretic peptides, bradykinin, and adrenomedullin [4]. Inhibition of neprilysin augments these beneficial peptides, promoting natriuresis, vasodilation, and antifibrotic effects, while simultaneous angiotensin receptor blockade counteracts the deleterious effects of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system [5]. Sacubitril is a prodrug converted to its active metabolite LBQ657, which inhibits neprilysin, whereas valsartan blocks the angiotensin II type 1 receptor [6]. An earlier strategy combining neprilysin inhibition with ACE inhibition (omapatrilat) was abandoned due to an unacceptable risk of angioedema, attributed to dual bradykinin accumulation [7].

## Pivotal Clinical Trial Evidence

The landmark PARADIGM-HF trial randomized 8,442 patients with HFrEF (NYHA class II–IV, ejection fraction ≤40%, later ≤35%) to sacubitril/valsartan or enalapril [8]. The trial was stopped early for benefit; sacubitril/valsartan reduced the primary composite of cardiovascular death or HF hospitalization by 20%, with significant reductions in all-cause mortality [8]. Subsequent analyses demonstrated reductions in sudden cardiac death and progressive pump failure death [9], as well as improvements in health-related quality of life [10]. The benefit was consistent across subgroups, including the elderly and those with diabetes [11,12].

The PIONEER-HF trial extended these findings to patients hospitalized with acute decompensated HFrEF, demonstrating a greater reduction in N-terminal pro-B-type natriuretic peptide (NT-proBNP) compared with enalapril, with a favorable safety profile [13]. The TRANSITION study confirmed feasibility of in-hospital initiation [14]. These data supported earlier initiation of ARNI therapy following stabilization [15].

## Heart Failure with Preserved Ejection Fraction

The role of ARNI in HF with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF) is less definitive. The PARAGON-HF trial randomized patients with ejection fraction ≥45% to sacubitril/valsartan or valsartan and narrowly missed its primary endpoint of total HF hospitalizations and cardiovascular death [16]. However, prespecified subgroup analyses suggested benefit in those with lower ejection fraction (below normal range) and in women [17]. A pooled analysis of PARADIGM-HF and PARAGON-HF supported a continuum of benefit that diminishes with increasing ejection fraction [18]. These observations influenced regulatory labeling and guideline recommendations for HF with mildly reduced ejection fraction [19].

## Guideline Recommendations

Contemporary guidelines from the American College of Cardiology/American Heart Association and the European Society of Cardiology endorse sacubitril/valsartan as foundational therapy for HFrEF, with consideration of de novo initiation rather than transition from an ACE inhibitor [19,20]. ARNI is now positioned among the four pillars of guideline-directed medical therapy, alongside beta-blockers, MRAs, and sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 inhibitors [21].

## Safety and Tolerability

Sacubitril/valsartan is generally well tolerated. The most common adverse effects include hypotension, hyperkalemia, and renal dysfunction, although renal outcomes were favorable relative to enalapril in PARADIGM-HF [22]. Angioedema occurred infrequently but mandates a 36-hour washout period when switching from an ACE inhibitor [8]. Theoretical concerns regarding neprilysin inhibition and amyloid-beta accumulation have not translated into demonstrable cognitive harm in the PERSPECTIVE trial [23].

## Additional Effects and Real-World Data

Beyond clinical endpoints, sacubitril/valsartan promotes reverse cardiac remodeling, as demonstrated in the PROVE-HF study, with reductions in left ventricular volumes and improvements in ejection fraction correlating with NT-proBNP decline [24]. The EVALUATE-HF study showed favorable effects on aortic stiffness and cardiac structure [25]. Real-world registries have confirmed effectiveness and tolerability outside the trial setting [26]. Cost-effectiveness analyses generally support value, though affordability remains a barrier to broader uptake [27].

## Ongoing Questions and Future Directions

Underutilization and clinical inertia limit the population-level impact of ARNI therapy [28]. Optimizing dose titration, sequencing among the four pillars, and identifying responders remain active areas of research [29]. Emerging data continue to refine its role across the spectrum of ejection fraction and in special populations, including post-myocardial infarction patients, where PARADISE-MI did not show significant benefit over ramipril [30].

## Conclusion

Sacubitril/valsartan has firmly established itself as a cornerstone of HFrEF therapy, offering mortality and morbidity benefits beyond conventional renin-angiotensin blockade. While its role in HFpEF is more nuanced, accumulating evidence supports a broad application across reduced and mildly reduced ejection fraction. Continued efforts to improve implementation are essential to realize its full clinical potential.
